sections.title: Reading Passage
sections.passage:
The concept of urban farming has gained significant traction in recent decades. As cities expand and populations grow, the demand for locally sourced food has increased dramatically. Urban farms range from small rooftop gardens to large-scale vertical farming operations that use artificial lighting and hydroponic systems to grow crops without soil.

Proponents of urban farming argue that it reduces the carbon footprint associated with transporting food from rural areas to cities. A head of lettuce grown on a rooftop in New York, for instance, does not need to travel thousands of kilometres before reaching a consumer's plate. Furthermore, urban farms can transform unused or abandoned spaces into productive green areas, improving air quality and reducing the urban heat island effect.

Critics, however, point out that urban farming is not without its challenges. The cost of setting up and maintaining a vertical farm can be prohibitively expensive, and the energy required to power artificial lighting systems may offset the environmental benefits. Additionally, urban farms typically produce a limited variety of crops, making it difficult to replace conventional agriculture entirely.

Despite these challenges, many city governments around the world are investing in urban agriculture programmes. Singapore, for example, has set a goal to produce thirty percent of its nutritional needs locally by 2030. Whether urban farming can truly transform the global food system remains to be seen, but its role as a supplement to traditional agriculture appears increasingly secure.
